newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco chief testifys for first time that cigarettes cause cancer.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco chief testifys for first time that cigarettes cause cancer.

text.p: The owner of America's fifth-largest tobacco company shook up a $5 billion secondhand-smoke trial on Monday by testifying that cigarettes cause cancer and that industry leader Philip Morris Cos. Inc. funded his struggling firm's anti-smoking lawsuits before its break with Big Tobacco.

Bennett LeBow, chairman of Brooke Group Ltd., which owns cigarette-maker Liggett Group, is the only U.S. tobacco chief executive to publicly acknowledge decades of medical research has rightly concluded that smoking causes lung cancer and other diseases.
"The answer is 'Yes,'" LeBow said when asked by plaintiffs attorney Stanely Rosenblatt if cigarette smoking caused cancer.
"Yes, we believe that for many people smoking cigarettes is very addictive," LeBow said in response to another question.

Both the health risk and the purported addictive nature of cigarettes are key claims by the 60,000 nonsmoking airline flight attendants claiming their respiratory and other ailments were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke aboard U.S. airlines.
The tobacco companies deny secondhand smoke is a health danger and say the flight attendants' exposure was trivial.

James Morgan, the head of Philip Morris's U.S. cigarette business, said in a videotape shown to the jury last week that the health risks of cigarettes were not certain and that smoking fell short of being truly addictive.

Liggett and parent Brooke are defendants along with five other cigarette makers and two trade groups in the secondhand-smoke trial but stand apart from the others, primarily because Liggett and LeBow have cooperated closely with anti-tobacco forces suing the industry in exchange for shelter from some lawsuits.

LeBow also testified that Philip Morris for several months in 1995 -- before Liggett struck the first of two deals with state attorneys general suing the tobacco industry -- had paid Liggett's legal fees.
He did not detail how much Philip Morris paid but said the company in 1995 was spending almost $10 million a year on lawyers.
"Philip Morris offered to pay all these fees," LeBow said.

LeBow gave few other details but said Philip Morris, the richest and most successful of the tobacco companies, stopped paying the fees after a few months. Liggett is the smallest of the top five U.S. tobacco company and has the shakiest finances, according to industry analysts.
Lawyers defending tobacco companies in the trial repeatedly interrupted LeBow but spent only a few minutes cross-examining him and did not mention the two deals he did with state attorneys general.
The tobacco lawyers had persuaded the trial judge to forbid mention of the settlements on grounds such testmony would prejudice the jurors.
Liggett made two separate agreements with anti-tobacco forces and is cooperating with legal and regulatory initiatives against cigarettes.
The deals were crucial in bringing about the tentative $368.5 billion settlement announced last month between tobacco companies and state attorneys general suing cigarette makers.
Edward Moss, a lawyer for Brown & Williamson Tobacco, questioned LeBow about why he had changed his thinking on smoking's health risks.
LeBow said he had hired lawyers and others to review research on smoking and had changed his mind during the past four years.
"I believe we absolutely did the right thing. We'd do it again in a minute," he said when a lawyer for Liggett questioned him.
Analysts have said LeBow, a financier with varied business holdings, struck the deals as a bid to save Liggett money and dress the company up for possible sale.
LeBow has since attacked the $368.5 billion pact, saying its terms would destroy Liggett.

LeBow said Liggett, maker of L&M, Chesterfield and more than 100 little-advertised discount brands of cigarettes, would in a few months reveal to Massachusetts regulators all the ingredients in Liggett cigarettes.
Other manufacturers refuse to detail their cigarettes' contents.
After his testimony, his first in a trial since publicly saying last spring that smoking was dangerous, LeBow declined to answer questions from reporters.

A lung surgeon, Edward Staples of Gainesville, Florida, showed the jurors samples of diseased lungs and other organs he brought to to the courthouse in a supermarket sack and testified that secondhand smoke was undeniably a cause of emphysema, lung cancer and other ailments.
"There's no question in my mind or among the physicians I work with. There is a general consensus," Staples said.

His testimony, coming during the second week of testimony in Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris et al, echoed the opinions of a former U.S. surgeon general and other experts who spoke last week. Testimony is expected to continue into September.
